source_fact_map.fact: The UK government fact sheet described an identity-concealment offence tied to a police-designated locality.
source_fact_map.quote: This measure will criminalise the act of wearing or otherwise using an item (for instance a face covering) that conceals their or another person’s identity when in an area that the police have designated.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: This measure will criminalise the act of wearing or otherwise using an item (for instance a face covering) that conceals their or another person’s identity when in an area that the police have designated. A designation can only be made in relation to an area when the police reasonably believe that a protest may or is taking place in that area, the protest is likely to involve or has involved the commission of offences and that a designation would prevent or control the commission of offences.

source_fact_map.fact: The Commons committee text described health, religious-observance, and work defenses for the proposed offense.
source_fact_map.quote: It is a defence for a person to prove that they wore or used the item for a purpose related to either the health of the person or others, religious observance or the person’s work.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Clause 86 introduces a new criminal offence for a person “wearing or otherwise using an item that conceals their identity or another person’s identity” in a public place that has been designated by the police. It is a defence for a person to prove that they wore or used the item for a purpose related to either the health of the person or others, religious observance or the person’s work. Clause 87 provides that a constable whose rank is at least that of inspector may designate a locality in England or Wales for a specified period.

children.title: Treasury Describes Read-Only Access to Fiscal Service Payment Data
children.subcategory: Federal payment systems and data access
children.description_short: Treasury said staff working with Tom Krause would have read-only access to coded Fiscal Service payment-system data.
children.description_medium: On February 4, Treasury told Congress that its staff working with Treasury employee Tom Krause would have read-only access to coded data in Bureau of the Fiscal Service payment systems. Treasury said its review had not delayed or rerouted Social Security or Medicare payments, and that agencies continued to direct their own payment processes. The source does not establish access to SSA records.
children.description_long: On February 4, 2025, Treasury sent Congress a description of its review of Bureau of the Fiscal Service payment systems. The department said Treasury staff working with Tom Krause would have read-only access to coded data in those systems. Treasury also said the review had not caused Social Security or Medicare payments to be delayed or redirected, and that the agency responsible for a payment continued to drive the process. This supports a limited account of read-only access to Treasury payment-system data. It does not establish that SSA granted DOGE access to SSA systems or that anyone accessed Social Security recipients’ files. The packet cites a Reuters report identifying the access as connected to Elon Musk’s team, but the Reuters page could not be fetched during this repair; that attribution remains unverified here. Treasury’s payment systems process federal disbursements, including Social Security and Medicare, while the records described in the second child belong to the separate Social Security Administration. Keep the agencies and events distinct.

children.title: SSA Reports Revoking DOGE Team 1 Access to PII Systems Under a March 20 Order
children.description_short: SSA said it revoked DOGE Team 1 access to PII systems under a March 20 court order; its declaration says DOGE defendants never accessed SSA systems of record.
children.description_medium: On March 24, Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek told a court that SSA had revoked SSA DOGE Team 1 members’ access to systems containing personally identifiable information under the court’s March 20 temporary restraining order. The declaration names Enterprise Data Warehouse, Numident, Master Beneficiary Record and Supplemental Security Record, while stating that DOGE defendants had never accessed SSA systems of record.
children.description_long: On March 24, 2025, Acting Social Security Administration Commissioner Leland Dudek filed a declaration supporting the status report required by the court’s March 20 temporary restraining order. He wrote that SSA had revoked all SSA DOGE Team 1 members’ access to systems containing personally identifiable information or systems of record. The declaration names the Enterprise Data Warehouse, Numident, Master Beneficiary Record, and Supplemental Security Record. It separately states that DOGE defendants had never had access to SSA systems of record. This evidence supports a narrow account of SSA’s access restrictions and reported compliance; it does not establish which individual previously viewed which information, whether data was copied or misused, or that the court made a final finding of unlawful access. The event is distinct from the February Treasury letter: Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service described read-only access to its payment-system data, whereas this declaration concerns SSA systems and a separate court order. The supplied February 18 date therefore does not describe either child accurately. Use March 24 for this declaration-based event and preserve the distinction between SSA DOGE Team 1 members and DOGE defendants, whom the declaration says had never accessed SSA systems of record.

title: At the 2016 Debate, Trump Said He Would Cut Taxes “Big League”
description_short: The official transcript records Trump saying “big league,” not “bigly,” while discussing taxes and regulation at the September 2016 debate.
description_medium: At the September 26, 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, Trump argued about taxes and regulation. The Commission on Presidential Debates transcript records him saying, “I’m going to cut taxes big league,” and then saying Clinton would “raise taxes big league.” It does not record the word “bigly,” so this entry should use “big league” and avoid claims about audience reaction or Trump’s language ability that the transcript does not establish.
description_long: During the first 2016 presidential debate at Hofstra University, moderator Lester Holt moved the candidates through a discussion of prosperity and economic plans. In that exchange, Donald Trump criticized Hillary Clinton’s tax and regulatory proposals, then said: “I’m going to cut regulations. I’m going to cut taxes big league, and you’re going to raise taxes big league, end of story.” The Commission on Presidential Debates transcript therefore supports “big league” as the phrase used in this sentence. It does not support a claim that Trump said “bigly” here. This correction is narrow: it records the wording in the official transcript and does not decide what Trump intended, whether listeners misheard it, or how widely a later interpretation circulated. The packet offers no verified evidence for the old card’s claims that this phrase became a viral phenomenon or a measure of Trump’s vocabulary. Treat this as an accurately quoted debate remark, not as evidence of a policy, legal violation, or lasting public effect.
